pass_a_gloss: Now let us show that we longed for knowledge on account of works fitting to the knowledge. Let all purity, the one from every defilement whatsoever, the one in any sin whatsoever, be made manifest in us. As sons of a long-tempered God and brothers of a long-tempered Christ, let us be long-tempered in all the things that befall; for a long-tempered man is much in prudence, but the small-souled one is strongly senseless. If it is necessary to set oneself forth through the arms of the righteousness, the right ones and the left ones, having set ourselves forth through glory, and not having been puffed up upon it, now let us also endure the dishonour; but if indeed we conducted our citizenship worthily of good speaking and were spoken well of, now let us also bear with the evil speaking from the irreverent. And still, if as true we were wondered at among the lovers of truth, now upon our being said to wander let us laugh. Upon many dangers, from which we were dragged free, many said that we were recognised by God; now let the one wishing say that we are not known, when perhaps rather we are being recognised. Carrying, then, the things that befall, we are being trained but we are not being put to death, and we, the rejoicing ones, are being made like to grieving ones.
pass_b_english: Now let us show that we have desired knowledge for the sake of works that befit knowledge. Let every kind of purity be made plain in us: purity from every defilement whatever, in whatever sin it lies. As sons of a long-suffering God and brothers of a long-suffering Christ, let us be long-suffering in all that happens to us; for “a long-suffering man is great in understanding, but the faint-hearted man is utterly foolish” (Proverbs 14:29). If a man must commend himself “by the weapons of righteousness, for the right hand and for the left” (2 Corinthians 6:7), then, having commended ourselves “through glory” (2 Corinthians 6:8) without growing vain over it, let us now endure dishonour as well. And if we have lived in a way that deserved good report, and were well spoken of, let us now bear the ill report of the ungodly too.

Further, if we were admired as truthful by those who love the truth, let us now laugh when it is said that we have gone astray. In many dangers from which we were rescued, many people said that we were acknowledged by God; now let anyone who likes say that we are unknown, at a time when perhaps we are more fully acknowledged. So, bearing what happens to us, we are “disciplined but not put to death” (2 Corinthians 6:9), and we who rejoice look like those who grieve.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 43); the old English was a digest: it quoted 2 Corinthians 6:4-10 as a block and invented 'honour won by confession', 'torturers' and 'good report of angels', none of which is in the Greek.
'ὁποιῶωδήποτε ἁμαρτήματε' read as 'ὁποιῳδήποτε ἁμαρτήματι'; 'un χαυνωθέντες' as 'μὴ χαυνωθέντες'; 'ἔτε' as 'ἔτι'; 'ἐπιγεινώσκεσθαι' as 'ἐπιγινώσκεσθαι'; 'all εἰ' as 'ἀλλ᾽ εἰ'.
'that we have gone astray' (passive/middle 'to wander, be led astray'), answering 2 Corinthians 6:8 'as deceivers'.
